Explained: How Extreme Heat Is Costing South Asia 31 Million Jobs Every Year
When we think about extreme heat, we usually think about discomfort, heatwaves and record-breaking temperatures.
The World Bank says we should also be thinking about jobs, wages and economic growth. According to a new report, extreme heat is already costing South Asia the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs every year. Without stronger adaptation measures, the region's economy could be nearly 7% smaller by 2050, making it the worst-hit developing region in the world.
Here's what the report says.
How is extreme heat costing millions of jobs?
The report says heat reduces the number of hours people can safely work, particularly in outdoor and physically demanding occupations such as construction, agriculture, manufacturing and transport. As temperatures rise, workers become less productive, businesses lose output and employers create fewer new jobs. Taken together, those losses already amount to the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs every year across South Asia.
Why is South Asia especially vulnerable?
South Asia combines three major risk factors: rising temperatures, densely populated cities and a large workforce employed in heat-exposed sectors. The region is also expected to add around 280 million working-age people by 2050, just as extreme heat is making it harder to create productive employment.
What does this mean for India's economy?
For India, the findings come at a critical time. The country is pushing ambitious goals under Viksit Bharat 2047, expanding manufacturing through Make in India and aiming to generate millions of jobs. The World Bank warns that unchecked heat could become a structural constraint on productivity, urban livability and long-term economic growth, potentially slowing those ambitions.
Could extreme heat also create new jobs?
Yes. The report says adapting to rising temperatures will also create economic opportunities. India is preparing the AHEAD (Alleviating Heat Stress by Enhancing Production of Affordable Cooling Devices) programme with World Bank support, which could boost domestic manufacturing of affordable cooling technologies and create nearly 3.7 million jobs by 2040. Demand for cooling solutions, climate-resilient construction and heat-resilient infrastructure is also expected to grow.
Can cities still avoid the worst impact?
The World Bank believes they can—but only if action begins now. Nearly 70% of the urban infrastructure India will need by mid-century has not yet been built, giving policymakers a rare opportunity to design cities that are better equipped to cope with rising temperatures. The report calls for greater investment in heat-resilient infrastructure, stronger Heat Action Plans, early warning systems, sustainable cooling technologies and better protection for vulnerable workers.
Why does this matter?
The report delivers a simple but powerful message: Extreme heat is no longer just an environmental problem. It's becoming an economic one. The challenge is no longer limited to surviving hotter summers. It is about protecting jobs, sustaining productivity and ensuring that rising temperatures do not derail South Asia's long-term growth ambitions.
(With inputs from ANI)

articles.title: ‘Was this heatwave caused by climate change?’ – we’re asking the wrong question - The Conversation

articles.full_text:
As the UK has baked through extreme heatwaves this summer, the same question has echoed across television studios and radio interviews: “Was this heatwave caused by climate change?”
It’s the wrong question.
Heatwaves have always happened. They are a natural part of our weather, driven by persistent high-pressure systems. Climate change did not create the June 2026 heatwave any more than it created the famous summer of 1976.
The question is not whether climate change caused the heatwave, but how much hotter and more dangerous heatwaves have become because greenhouse gases, primarily from burning fossil fuels, have accumulated in the atmosphere.
This is the focus of attribution science, which analyses how much hotter a heatwave has become because of these extra greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. It has transformed how climate scientists understand extreme weather. Now our public conversation needs to catch up.
The missing words in the climate conversation are not human-caused climate change, but fossil fuel emissions.
Every heatwave today develops in a warmer atmosphere containing far more greenhouse gases than it did a century ago. This makes every heatwave today hotter than it would have been without those additional emissions.
Our research illustrates this vividly. When we recreated the atmospheric conditions of the 1976 UK heatwave under today’s climate, peak temperatures were around 3-4°C higher. The weather pattern was the same; the climate in which it occurred had changed.
Climate change does not create heatwaves. It loads the dice. Weather variability still determines whether a heatwave occurs, but greenhouse gases released from burning fossil fuels make heatwaves hotter, more likely to break records, and more damaging, to health and infrastructure alike. The same principle applies to heavy rainfall, drought and coastal flooding.
The physics is remarkably simple. The atmosphere doesn’t care about politics. It responds to the concentration of greenhouse gases. Every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning coal, oil and gas adds to that concentration and shifts the odds towards more damaging extreme weather.
Yet this is rarely how we talk about climate change.
Scientists and journalists often use the phrase “human-caused climate change”. It is scientifically correct, but it describes the consequence rather than the mechanism. It can also make people think first about their own behaviour: the flight they took last summer, whether they recycled or should drive less.
Individual choices matter. But they are not where the story begins.
The story begins with fossil fuels.
Burning fossil fuels accounts for around three-quarters of global greenhouse gas emissions and almost 90% of carbon dioxide emissions. Their cumulative emissions have altered the Earth’s energy balance and changed the climate in which every weather event now unfolds.
One reason this simple physical story became blurred was the success of the personal carbon footprint. Popularised by BP’s “Beyond Petroleum” campaign in the early 2000s, it encouraged people to focus on their own emissions.
This is not about absolving individuals of responsibility. Personal choices and actions are part of the solution. But this campaign shifted public attention away from the much larger challenge of transforming the fossil-fuel energy systems responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions. No amount of shorter showers or diligent recycling can substitute for decarbonising electricity, transport, industry and domestic heating.
So, rather than asking whether climate change caused a heatwave, we should be explaining that greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels are accumulating in the atmosphere, trapping heat and amplifying extreme weather. This makes all heatwaves hotter, more likely and more dangerous. Heatwaves will continue to get hotter until these fossil fuel emissions stop accumulating.
The record-breaking European heatwaves and wildfires of 2026 show us that climate change is no longer a distant threat. It is shaping the weather outside our windows today. The atmosphere will continue to respond to greenhouse gas concentrations, regardless of politics or public debate.
The climate we live in today is the least extreme climate you will experience in your lifetimes because of ongoing fossil fuel emissions.
The public conversation needs to catch up with the science. If we are serious about limiting future warming, we must rapidly reduce fossil fuel emissions while making our homes, infrastructure and communities more resilient to the climate change that is already here.

New Delhi [India], July 31 (ANI): Extreme heat is costing South Asia the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs every year and could shrink the region's economy by nearly 7 per cent by 2050 if countries do not take adaptation measures, according to a new World Bank report. The report warned that rising temperatures are emerging as a major threat to employment, productivity and long-term economic growth.
Releasing its report, 'A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities', the World Bank said, "Extreme heat already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs a year across South Asia,"while "without adaptation, rising heat could leave South Asia's GDP close to 7 per cent smaller by 2050, the steepest projected loss of any developing region."
The report said South Asia is expected to add around 280 million working-age people by 2050, but rising temperatures are making it harder to create productive jobs by reducing labour productivity, lowering earnings and discouraging investment. "Heat reduces productivity in existing work, discourages the investment that would create new jobs, and shifts labour demand toward cooling and heat-resilient industries," it said.
World Bank Vice President for South Asia Johannes Zutt said, "South Asia's cities are central to the region's future, but rising temperatures are putting jobs, livelihoods, and economic growth at risk."
For India, the findings come as the government is pursuing ambitious long-term growth plans, including its vision of becoming a developed nation under the Viksit Bharat 2047 roadmap, expanding manufacturing under Make in India, strengthening global supply chain participation and creating millions of new jobs. The report cautions that rising temperatures could undermine these efforts by becoming "a structural constraint on productivity, livability, and economic growth," particularly as cities continue to expand.
The report also noted that around 70 per cent of the urban infrastructure India will need by mid-century is yet to be built, giving policymakers an opportunity to integrate heat resilience into future housing, transport and urban infrastructure. It added that India is preparing the Alleviating Heat Stress by Enhancing Production of Affordable Cooling Devices (AHEAD) programme with World Bank support, which could help expand domestic manufacturing of affordable cooling equipment and create close to 3.7 million jobs by 2040.
Calling for heat to be treated as a development priority rather than a seasonal emergency, the report recommended investing in heat-resilient infrastructure, strengthening Heat Action Plans, expanding early warning systems, protecting vulnerable workers, promoting sustainable cooling and mobilising greater public and private investment to help cities remain productive and competitive in a warming climate. (ANI)

Extreme heat is turning into a threat to economy
Extreme heat is no longer merely an environmental concern; it has become a serious economic challenge for countries like Bangladesh. A new World Bank report has once again revealed how the consequences of extreme heat are being felt in lost jobs, lower productivity, and slower economic growth. According to the report, heat-induced productivity losses cost Bangladesh an estimated $1.3-1.8 billion in 2024, equivalent to 0.3-0.4 percent of the country's GDP. The losses rise sharply on days when temperatures exceed 37 degrees Celcius. The impact is particularly severe in Dhaka, where extreme heat renders 3 percent of working hours unworkable, wiping out the equivalent of 465,000 full-time jobs annually. As temperatures continue to rise, these losses are projected to more than double by 2080.
Unfortunately, global climate commitments continue to fall short to address this crisis, while geopolitical tensions, wars, and competing economic priorities complicate international climate action. As wealthier nations remain divided over emissions reductions and climate finance, countries like Bangladesh, despite contributing very little to global emissions, are paying an increasingly heavy price.
The World Bank report makes it clear that the burden of rising temperatures falls disproportionately on those least able to cope. Low-income households, informal workers, women, children, and the elderly are among the hardest hit. Labour-intensive sectors such as construction, transport, agriculture, and particularly the RMG industry face mounting risks as workers struggle to maintain productivity under increasingly dangerous conditions. The report's finding that heat stress in RMG factories has been linked to a greater risk of violence and harassment against women workers who fail to meet production targets is alarming.
There are, however, reasons for cautious optimism. The report highlights Bangladesh's Green Transformation Fund and the remarkable growth in Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED)-certified RMG factories as examples of how targeted investments can improve energy efficiency, working conditions, and industrial resilience. These initiatives show that adaptation measures are both feasible and economically worthwhile. But isolated successes are not enough. The country still lacks a comprehensive strategy to make its cities, workplaces, and infrastructure resilient to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves.
Therefore, the government must act urgently to address this crisis. It must expand urban green spaces, protect water bodies that naturally cool cities, enforce heat-sensitive building standards, improve ventilation in factories and workplaces, and strengthen occupational safety regulations to protect outdoor and industrial workers during periods of extreme heat. Employers should be encouraged to adopt flexible working hours where feasible, while the authorities should invest in effective early warning systems and public awareness campaigns. Continued support for cleaner industries and climate-resilient infrastructure is also necessary. Protecting our workers from extreme heat is essential for safeguarding jobs, sustaining investment, and securing the country's long-term development goals.

articles.title: Why children are more vulnerable to heatwaves than adults: Doctor explains the hidden risks of heat, humidity and dehydration - The Times of India
articles.search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Why children are vulnerable to heat-related illnesses
Most parents look at the weather app before deciding whether it is safe for their children to play outside. If the temperature reads 40°C, there is instant concern. But if it shows 34°C, the day often feels less threatening. That number, however, tells only part of the story.
Humidity changes everything.
A hot, humid afternoon can put much more strain on the body than a hotter but drier day because it becomes harder to cool down naturally. This is becoming an increasingly important public health issue as India witnesses longer, more intense heatwaves and rising humidity. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) and the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) have repeatedly highlighted the growing health risks associated with extreme heat.
For children, the risks are even greater.
"They are not simply smaller adults," said Dr Ankit Desai, Paediatric Anaesthetist and Founder & Director, Children's Anaesthesia Services. "Children's bodies regulate temperature very differently, leaving them with a much narrower safety margin when exposed to heat."
2/7
The invisible danger: When humidity turns heat into a health risk
Most people believe sweating automatically cools the body. It does, but only when sweat evaporates.
When humidity is high, the air is already packed with moisture. Sweat stays on the skin instead of evaporating efficiently. The body continues producing sweat, but loses one of its most effective cooling systems. As internal temperature rises, dehydration develops faster and heat-related illnesses become more likely.
Dr Desai explained, "Heat alone is not sufficient for narrating the full story. The combination of high temperature and high humidity gives rise to conditions where the human body struggles to cool itself. This situation is commonly referred to as the 'wet-bulb effect,' which is becoming increasingly important with weather change causing more frequent and prolonged heatwaves across India."
Researchers have increasingly warned that combinations of heat and humidity can become dangerous even when temperatures do not appear extreme. India's heat action plans have also started paying greater attention to the heat index, which reflects how hot conditions actually feel when humidity is included.
The result can be dehydration, painful muscle cramps, heat exhaustion and, in severe cases, heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency that can damage the brain, heart, kidneys and other vital organs if treatment is delayed.
3/7
Why a child's body struggles more than an adult's
Children's bodies are built for growth, not for handling extreme heat. Their skin surface is larger compared to their body weight, which means they absorb heat from the environment more quickly. At the same time, their sweat glands are still developing and are less efficient than those of adults. They produce less sweat, reducing the body's ability to cool itself.
Dr Desai said, "There are several cases that witness how differently children's bodies regulate temperature in comparison to adults. Whether it is the heat outside or maintaining the right body temperature inside an operating room, children's bodies have a much narrower margin for error."
Young children also depend almost entirely on adults for basic needs such as drinking water. Unlike adults, they often do not realise they are thirsty. They become absorbed in games, sports or outdoor activities and continue running even as dehydration begins.
Infants face an even bigger challenge. They cannot ask for water, describe dizziness or explain that they feel unusually hot. Their discomfort may appear only as excessive crying, unusual sleepiness or refusing feeds.
Physical activity adds another layer of risk. A football match during afternoon recess or a long play session in humid weather can rapidly increase body temperature, overwhelming a child's natural cooling system before anyone notices.
4/7
The first warning signs are often easy to miss
Heat-related illnesses rarely begin dramatically. Instead, they often look like an ordinary bad day.
A child may seem unusually quiet, complain of a headache, become irritable or lose interest in playing. Some develop dizziness, nausea, vomiting or painful muscle cramps. Others may have a rapid heartbeat or urinate much less than usual because the body is conserving water.
Dr Desai cautioned that parents should watch for excessive tiredness, unusual irritability, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps, rapid heartbeat and reduced urination. Younger children may become sleepy, restless or refuse feeds.
The most dangerous stage is heat stroke.
If a child becomes confused, loses consciousness, develops seizures or has a very high body temperature, it is a medical emergency. Immediate cooling measures should begin while urgent medical care is arranged.
5/7
Protecting children starts long before they feel thirsty
Waiting for children to ask for water is often too late. Good protection begins before symptoms appear.
Children should drink fluids regularly throughout the day, especially during hot weather and outdoor activities. Schools can help by scheduling regular water breaks rather than expecting children to remember on their own.
Light-coloured, loose-fitting cotton clothes improve airflow around the body and reduce heat build-up. Outdoor sports should be limited during the hottest and most humid hours whenever possible. Shade, rest breaks and cool drinking water are simple interventions that can prevent serious illness.
Dr Desai emphasised, "Schools and parents need to keep track of water breaks, particularly during outdoor activities. Wearing lightweight, loose-fitting cotton clothes helps improve air circulation and cooling."
Parents should also remember that indoor heat can become dangerous. Poorly ventilated homes may trap heat for hours, especially during prolonged heatwaves.
One rule deserves repeating every summer: never leave an infant or child inside a parked vehicle, even for a few minutes. Temperatures inside cars rise extremely quickly and can become fatal within a short time.
6/7
What an operating room teaches us about children's bodies
Interestingly, doctors think about body temperature long before children step outside into the summer heat. Inside an operating theatre, the concern is often the exact opposite.
Instead of overheating, children lose body heat much faster than adults during surgery. Anaesthesia interferes with the body's ability to regulate temperature, making young patients vulnerable to hypothermia.
Dr Desai explained, "As children have a larger surface area relative to their body mass and limited energy reserves, even small drops in body temperature during surgery can increase the risk of complications, delay recovery and affect healing."
This is why paediatric operating rooms use warming blankets, warmed intravenous fluids, continuous temperature monitoring and carefully controlled room temperatures.
The lesson extends far beyond surgery. Whether protecting a child from scorching playgrounds or maintaining warmth during an operation, the principle remains the same: children require specialised care because their bodies respond to temperature differently.
7/7
Medical experts consulted
This article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:
Dr Ankit Desai, Paediatric Anaesthetist and Founder & Director, Children's Anaesthesia Services.
Inputs were used to explain why children are more vulnerable to heat-related illnesses, how heat and humidity affect their bodies differently, and what parents can do to protect them.

articles.title: Heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke: Cenla doctor explains the warning signs - KALB | News Channel 5
articles.search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
ALEXANDRIA, La. (KALB) - Medical experts warn that confusing heat exhaustion with heat stroke is a mistake that can be fatal, and the difference between the two conditions comes down to how a person is behaving.
Rapides Regional Medical Center Emergency Department Medical Director Dr. Brent Arnold said the key warning sign is in the name itself.
“The main difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke is when we start having confusion or altered mental status,” Arnold said. “It’s kind of been the word stroke. We typically think of ischemic strokes or blood clot type strokes. And that can cause slurred speech, trouble walking, weakness, passing out.”
Once confusion, altered mental status, or seizures set in, Arnold said it is a true medical emergency. Without immediate treatment, heat stroke is fatal up to 30% of the time.
Arnold also cautioned against a common misconception — that a person must stop sweating to be in serious danger.
“The other kind of key thing we used to talk about some was the absence of sweating,” Arnold said. “You can have a heat stroke and someone still be sweating heavily. In the opposite, so much if you’re so dehydrated and have been hot long enough that you’re not sweating anymore, that in and of itself would be a reason to come in too.”
Medical experts say anyone showing signs of confusion, slurred speech, or weakness in the heat should not be left to cool down on their own. Call 911 immediately.

Swift Current remains under a yellow heat warning issued by Environment and Climate Change Canada.
Daytime highs are expected to reach 32 C over the next two days, while overnight lows will only cool to around 16 C, providing little relief from the heat.
Dangerous symptoms
Environment Canada warns that prolonged periods of elevated temperatures increase the risk of heat-related illnesses, including heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Symptoms can include nausea, fatigue, dizziness, dark-coloured urine and sudden changes in consciousness. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should move to a cool, shaded or air-conditioned location and drink water.
Heat stroke is a serious medical emergency. If you or someone you know is experiencing symptoms, seek medical aid or call 911.

articles.title: Gujarat rain batters Surat as red alert issued for 13 districts - The New Indian Express
articles.search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
AHMEDABAD: Gujarat's monsoon intensified on Friday as torrential rain lashed Surat and large parts of South Gujarat, flooding low lying areas, disrupting traffic and prompting the administration to step up emergency measures after the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for 13 districts.
Heavy rain battered Surat from the morning of July 31, rapidly turning several parts of the city into waterlogged zones. Areas including VIP Road, Pandesara, Katargam and Dabholi were inundated, while the overflowing Bhedawad creek heightened the flood threat.
The situation was particularly serious as Surat and several neighbouring districts had already been affected by repeated spells of heavy rain.
The latest weather system has triggered a fresh round of precautionary measures across the region, with authorities advising residents to avoid unnecessary travel.
The IMD has issued a red alert for 13 districts Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Anand, Narmada, Chhota Udepur, Bhavnagar, Botad, Bharuch, Valsad, Surat, Tapi, Dang and Navsari, warning of extremely heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning and squally winds.
The impact was not confined to Surat. Intense rainfall disrupted road traffic and normal life across several parts of Central and South Gujarat. On Friday, Umarpada in Surat recorded nearly eight inches of rain, while Borsad in Anand received more than six inches by noon, highlighting the intensity of the downpour.
With rivers and drainage systems under pressure, the state has shifted into a heightened disaster response mode. Seventeen National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams, 33 State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) platoons and six Army columns have been deployed, while more than 720 people have already been evacuated from vulnerable low lying areas in Vadodara, Surat, Anand and Narmada districts. Twenty one dams have also been placed on high alert as water levels continue to rise.
In Surat, the worsening conditions prompted the district administration to order the closure of all factories for two days to reduce movement and minimise risks to workers during the peak of the weather event.
The administration has also declared a holiday for all schools, colleges and anganwadis on August 1, with educational institutions remaining closed as the IMD forecasts another spell of heavy rain.
An Army team was sent from Vadodara to Surat to strengthen relief and rescue operations, adding military personnel to the existing disaster response machinery.
The administration has also cancelled the leave of all officers and employees with immediate effect to ensure that the government machinery remains fully operational during the crisis.
Health Minister Praful Panseria visited the Disaster Management Office and held a review meeting with senior officials, including the district Collector, to assess the evolving situation and coordinate the response.
Officials said the immediate priority was prevention, evacuation and rapid response rather than waiting for flooding to worsen.
People have been advised to remain indoors or move to safer locations and avoid unnecessary travel, particularly as heavy rain is expected to continue through the day and into the night.
The warning is especially significant for people living in low lying areas, near overflowing water bodies and along vulnerable roads, where even a short spell of heavy rain could quickly disrupt connectivity.
The latest spell follows an already damaging phase of the monsoon across Gujarat. Between July 23 and 27, widespread flooding and waterlogging forced the closure of 1,540 roads across the state, with South Gujarat accounting for 1,251 closures, the highest among all regions. Of these, 1,236 have been reopened, while traffic was restored on 1,187 roads within 24 to 48 hours.
That fragile recovery now faces another test.
Surat, Valsad, Navsari, Bharuch, Tapi and Dang remain among the key districts under close watch as the weather system moves westwards towards Gujarat.
The IMD has warned of another spell of heavy to very heavy rainfall between July 31 and August 1, with isolated places likely to receive extremely to exceptionally heavy rain.
The latest system is being driven by a deep depression over west central Chhattisgarh and adjoining Vidarbha and southeast Madhya Pradesh, which is expected to move westwards towards Gujarat while gradually weakening.
An active monsoon trough and an east-west shear zone across central India are also supporting widespread rainfall activity.
For Surat, however, the immediate concern is the sheer volume of water already accumulating across the city and district.
With creeks overflowing, low lying areas submerged and more rain forecast, authorities are racing against the next spell rather than waiting for the current flooding to recede.
The administration's precautionary shutdowns, deployment of rescue teams and cancellation of staff leave reflect the seriousness of the warning.
Gujarat is not facing an isolated spell of heavy rain, but another widespread monsoon challenge, with South Gujarat once again at the centre of the storm.

Guwahati (Assam) [India], July 31 (ANI): In view of the recent flood situation in the state, the Assam government has taken up various measures to provide additional relief to the flood-affected people.
The measures were also discussed in the state cabinet meeting held on Friday at Lok Sewa Bhawan in Guwahati under the chairmanship of Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma.
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Friday said that the State Government will shortly convene a meeting with public and private insurance companies to ensure the expeditious settlement of insurance claims relating to insured movable and immovable properties damaged in the recent floods in the districts of Sivasagar, Charaideo, Golaghat and Jorhat.
Chief Minister said, "A similar meeting will also be held with Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in this regard. To provide fresh school uniforms to students in the flood-affected districts, the State Government will release approximately Rs. 8 crore from the Chief Minister's Relief Fund to Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan. Meanwhile, the distribution of textbooks to students in these districts has commenced from yesterday."
"In addition, the process of collecting details of students affected by the floods has already begun. The State Government will expedite the damage assessment process arising from the recent floods so that financial assistance can be disbursed to the affected people within the month of August," the Chief Minister added.
He further said that the Government will provide financial assistance of Rs. 23 lakh each for the repair of educational institutions that have been damaged in the recent floods.
On the other hand, the State Cabinet has approved the Assam Animal Husbandry & Veterinary Subordinate Service (Amendment) Rules, 2026 to regulate recruitment and service conditions of Veterinary Field Assistants (VFA). The amendments will ensure transparency, merit-based selection, and uniformity in recruitment and service conditions of VFA.
"The State Cabinet has approved the Assam Compressed Biogas (CBG) Policy 2026, formulated in alignment with the national Model State CBG Policy, for a comprehensive framework designed to convert the state's organic waste into clean energy. The Commissionerate of Industries & Commerce is designated as the State Nodal Agency, and it is responsible for notifying the policy and managing the Single Window Portal for time-bound project execution. Comprehensive Incentive Framework under the Policy will provide : Capital subsidy of Rs. 0.50 crore per TPD of installed capacity, subject to a ceiling of Rs. 20 crore per project; Power Tariff Support of Rs. 2 per unit for 5 years; Land Support Measures
including Land allotment through dedicated land bank, Concessional lease of Government land, Facilitation of Panchayat land lease, Exemption from stamp duty, registration fee and land conversion charges; Fiscal Support Measures including reimbursement of up to 100% of net SGST for 5 years and Interest subsidy on term loans; Subsidy for biomass aggregation machinery, pollution control equipment subsidy, patent/trademark reimbursement and employment incentives," the Assam Chief Minister said.
He further said that the State Cabinet has approved the Assam Legal Metrology (Government Approved Test Centre) Rules, 2026 to implement Self-Certification by Manufacturers (through State GATC) and Third-Party Certification of Weighing and Measuring Instruments as part of the Government's compliance reduction and deregulation reforms, which have been drafted in line with the Central Government Approved Test Centre (GATC) Rules.
"The State Cabinet has approved the issuance of the final notification of Raikushni Proposed Reserved Forest (PRF) and Tharko Nalbari Proposed Reserved Forest (PRF) in Goalpara District as Reserved Forests (RF) under the provisions of the Assam Forest Regulation, 1891," the Chief Minister said. Orange alert issued for geological disaster risks in three provinces
China's Ministry of Natural Resources and the China Meteorological Administration jointly issued an orange alert for geological disaster risks at 6 pm on Friday, urging governments at all levels and relevant regions to step up preventive measures.
The authorities also advised the public to pay close attention to updated information and exercise caution when traveling to areas under alert.
According to the authorities, an orange alert has been issued for parts of northern Sichuan, southwestern Shaanxi, and southeastern Gansu. A yellow alert is in effect for parts of central-western Shanxi, central-southern Heilongjiang, southern Guangdong, southern Guangxi, northern and central-southern Sichuan, southwestern Shaanxi, and southeastern Gansu, from 8 pm Friday to 8 pm Saturday.
Residents in orange-alert zones who live near high-risk sites or threatened areas should immediately evacuate to nearby designated shelters as directed by local disaster response authorities, and those near slopes, cliffs, ravines, or waterways should follow evacuation signals and move to safety without delay.
People in yellow-alert zones should stay alert to any changes in warning information, pay attention to hazard signs in their vicinity, and avoid lingering in high-risk areas such as ravines, slopes, and steep cliffs.
China uses a four-tier, color-coded warning system for geological disaster risks, ranging from least to most severe: blue, yellow, orange, and red. Each level corresponds to escalating probability and potential impact of hazards such as landslides and mudslides. The orange alert, the second-highest level, signals a high risk of geological disasters. It triggers mandatory evacuation orders for residents in high-risk zones and requires local authorities to activate emergency response measures. In contrast, the yellow alert indicates a relatively high risk and calls for heightened vigilance and monitoring without mandatory relocation.

Summarized by AI; it may make mistakes. Check important info
Summarized by AI; it may make mistakes. Check important info
Monsoon activity escalated sharply across Gujarat on Friday, as relentless early-morning downpours hammering central and southern belts expanded rapidly into North Gujarat and the Saurashtra region by early afternoon.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has declared a Red Alert for heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across multiple districts under the influence of an active deep depression. Emergency data from the State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC) reveals a fast-moving, high-intensity deluge unfolding between 06:00 AM and 02:00 PM.
Surat’s Umarpada Crosses 240 mm in Eight-Hour Surge
Between 06:00 AM and 02:00 PM, 125 talukas across the state recorded measurable precipitation. Umarpada in Surat district bore the brunt of the onslaught, logging an extraordinary 247 mm (9.72 inches) of rain to lead the state’s cumulative tallies.
Other regions in South and Central Gujarat recorded massive accumulations over the same eight-hour window:
• Kheda District: Nadiad registered 191 mm (7.52 inches), triggering widespread urban waterlogging, while Vaso accumulated 177 mm (6.97 inches).
• Anand District: Intense spells pounded Borsad (170 mm), Khambhat (165 mm), Petlad (152 mm), and Anand taluka (151 mm).
• Narmada & Tapi Districts: Sagbara and Garudeshwar recorded 152 mm and 144 mm respectively, whilst Dolvan logged 149 mm.
Afternoon Shift: Cloudburst-like Intensity Hits Tribal Belt
As the day progressed, peak rainfall activity shifted heavily into the tribal and hilly regions of South Gujarat. Between 12:00 PM and 02:00 PM alone, 97 talukas registered fresh rainfall, with localized torrents dropping huge volumes in brief bursts:
• Ambika (Surat): Recorded a fierce 108 mm (4.25 inches) in just two hours—a rate exceeding 50 mm per hour.
• Dolvan (Tapi): Received 86 mm (3.39 inches) during the afternoon spell.
• Dangs & Navsari Belt: Subir in Dangs logged 80 mm, Vansada in Navsari saw 69 mm, and Valod in Tapi registered 64 mm.
Early-morning hotspots saw rainfall rates ease slightly, with Umarpada and Nadiad reporting 44 mm and 40 mm respectively during the midday hours.
Widespread Spells Reach Newer Talukas
The afternoon hours marked a distinct geographical expansion of the monsoon system beyond its initial focus in Central and South Gujarat:
• North Gujarat Expansion: Rain activity pushed northward into Sabarkantha (Himatnagar 20 mm, Talod 18 mm, Prantij 10 mm), Arvalli (Dhansura 19 mm, Sathamba, Shamlaji), Gandhinagar (Dehgam 15 mm), and parts of Mehsana (Visnagar, Vadnagar).
• Saurashtra Belt: Showers expanded into Bhavnagar (Ghogha 17 mm, Bhavnagar city 9 mm), Amreli (Lathi, Amreli city, Rajula), Botad (Botad, Gadhada), and Rajkot (Jasdan).
High Alert and Emergency Directives
With flash flood warnings active for saturated river catchments across Kheda, Anand, Narmada, Vadodara, and Tapi, local administrations remain on high readiness. Teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) have been deployed to vulnerable zones.
Disaster management authorities have urged residents in low-lying pockets to remain indoors, stay away from swollen water bodies, and strictly prohibited fishermen from venturing off the South Gujarat coast.

In the City of Buenos Aires and the Metropolitan Area of Buenos Aires (AMBA), the end of July presents concerning weather conditions. According to the National Meteorological Service (SMN), a yellow alert has been issued due to the presence of intense storms and strong wind gusts for this Friday, July 31.
Meteorological alert in Buenos Aires: forecast details
The morning in Buenos Aires begins with warm and humid weather. Minimum temperatures hover around 13°C, with humidity reaching 88%. The wind blows from the east, without affecting visibility.
As the day progresses, the weather is expected to deteriorate. Maximum temperatures could range between 18°C and 21°C, accompanied by an increasingly cloudy sky. During the afternoon and evening, storms will develop with accumulated precipitation that could exceed 50 mm in some areas of the Conurbano.
Strong wind gusts and electrical activity are expected, with a possibility of hail. The most severe storms are anticipated in the northern and western parts of Greater Buenos Aires during the afternoon, while in the south and the coast, precipitation will intensify at night.
Extended forecast: what to expect for the weekend
In addition to the alerts for Buenos Aires, the Early Warning System (SAT) maintains the warning for the northeast and center of the province, including the Atlantic Coast. These areas could experience heavy rains causing flooding.
Conversely, in the north of the country, warm temperatures are expected with highs around 30°C. However, in the south, the province of Santa Cruz is under an alert for extreme cold and snowfalls, with lows down to -10°C.
For Saturday, August 1, a cold front is expected to cause a drop in temperatures. The day will start unstable, with temperatures between 12°C and 18°C. On Sunday, temperatures will drop even further, ranging between 11°C and 14°C, under a partly cloudy sky.
The start of the next week will be marked by cold temperatures due to the entry of polar air. On Monday, August 3, temperatures will fluctuate between 10°C and 16°C, ensuring a typically wintry start to August in the central region.
